summary: The Verge reports that Discogs, the user-built database and marketplace for physical music media, is alienating its sellers after raising fees and charging them on shipping. Sellers cite old tech, bugs, poor support and a clumsy redesign, and some are shifting to eBay, Amazon or their own sites. They fear that fewer sellers will make the database less complete and turn a beloved community into another dysfunctional website.
one_line: Discogs' fee hike and fees on shipping, plus a buggy site and weak support, are driving sellers away and threatening its vinyl community and database.
key_facts: Discogs was founded in 2000 by Intel programmer Kevin Lewandowski, a few months before Wikipedia, and added its marketplace in the mid-aughts.
Sellers must submit a record's information to the database if it isn't already there in order to sell it, which is how the database became so complete.
On May 22nd, 2023, Discogs raised its seller fee from 8 to 9 percent and, for the first time, began charging that fee on shipping costs.
Discogs suggested sellers use a tool to raise all inventory prices by a percentage or offer free shipping, which sellers say results in the same money going to Discogs.
A European seller on the platform since 2008 does 80 percent of his business there, nets about €20,000 a month, and says his sales have shrunk by half over the past year; he is building his own site.

The fee increase came shortly before USPS raised Media Mail prices by an average of 7 percent, and a year after Discogs moved all transactions to PayPal, which charges higher fees on international purchases and requires tracking numbers.
Doug Martin, who sells mainly new vinyl, says eBay fees are about 1 percent higher than Discogs' but eBay brings roughly double his Discogs business, and it has grown since the fee rise.
The Connecticut seller, on Discogs since 2009, lowered prices to offset shipping costs and instituted an order minimum, a major shift for a marketplace known for records under $10 and even under $5.
Discogs attributed the fee increase to investments in regulatory compliance, including tax support and privacy protection, and declined to comment for the story.
Many sellers speculated that Discogs was trying to boost its valuation for a potential sale, following a since-deleted viral Twitter thread by Mike Simonetti lamenting 'the fall of discogs'.
Discogs held a late-August sale featuring only 11 of the site's largest stores, which Martin said would further depress prices for other sellers.
Martin says fewer new albums are being added to the database since the price increases, and UPCs he looks up are not there as often as they used to be.
The author waited from July 25th to August 23rd for a response to a request for a Discogs press contact.
